question: Must everyone die?
summary: Romans 5:12 says death passed upon all men through Adam. Hebrews 9:27 says it is appointed unto men once to die. Genesis 5:24 and Hebrews 11:5 then say Enoch was taken by God and did not see death — and 2 Kings 2:11 does the same for Elijah. The universal claim has named exceptions.

reconcile.connective: Commentators read the universal-death verses as the standing rule for fallen humanity, with Enoch and Elijah granted a God-wrought change that does the work of death without the dying.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptics' Annotated Bible presses the point directly: the flat universal claims of Romans 5:12 and Hebrews 9:27 cannot stand once Scripture itself records Enoch and Elijah being taken without dying.

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Unto men generally, during the course of the present world, not all men as some falsely quote; for Enoch and Elijah have not died, and those that shall be alive at the day of judgment shall not die, but be changed.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke explicitly answers the contradiction: he restricts the 'appointed once to die' clause to men 'generally,' names Enoch and Elijah as the exceptions, and rebukes reading the verse as universal ('not all men as some falsely quote').
excerpts.source_note_text:
As it is appointed - Αποκειται· It is laid before them by the Divine decree: Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return. Unto men generally, during the course of the present world, not all men as some falsely quote; for Enoch and Elijah have not died, and those that shall be alive at the day of judgment shall not die, but be changed.
But after this the judgment - They shall die but once, and be judged but once, therefore there is no metempsychosis, no transmigration from body to body; judgment succeeds to dying; and as they shall be judged but once, they can die but once.
